newsitem.title: UK: S&P sees "tremendous" prospects for Russian banks.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees "tremendous" prospects for Russian banks.

text.p: Russian banks have "tremendous" growth prospects but the industry has a high rate of failure, Standard & Poor's said in a report on Tuesday.
"Banks are beginning to take a grip on their infrastructure and managerial needs and future growth prospects are tremendous, with signs of real loan growth already visible," S&P said.

"Liquidity problems, reflecting a lack of confidence in most of the banks, are resulting in a high rate of failure and contributing to consolidation. Problem loans are difficult to quantify because of a lack of transparency in reporting," the agency said.

The development of Russia's banking system in the post-Soviet period has been marked by a dizzying pace of change and considerable financial opportunity, said S&P financial institutions ratings director Tanya Azarchs in the report.
On the collapse of the Soviet Union, three of five state owned banks privatised themselves. Low capital and regulatory requirements resulted in the creation of thousands of new banks.

"There is, however, a trend towards consolidation in the very fragmented system beyond Sberbank, the state-guaranteed savings bank which plays a dominant role. Consolidation will be essential to compete and service the larger commercial clients."
The low levels and short term nature of lending by Russian banks are typical for high-inflation economies and high real interest rate environments, Azarchs said.
"But there is a growth in real terms in bank lending, the future of which will depend on the banks' ability to make creditworthy loans," the report said.
"Many Russian banks have significant problem loan portfolios, the level of which is difficult to determine due to lack of disclosure and inconsistencies in accounting for loans," S&P added.
The agency said capital ratios appear high, but taking into consideration the riskiness of the operating environment and large equity portfolios, the risk-adjusted ratios are not high.
"The absolute levels of capital are also low," Azarchs said.
